results.evidence: APA §1.1: "'Products' means the products listed on Schedule 1.1(c) of the Disclosure Schedule." APA §2.4(d) excludes "any Liability arising out of or relating to Products manufactured or sold prior to the Closing, including any product liability, breach of warranty, personal injury or property damage claim, and any recall, market withdrawal or field correction of such Products." Schedule 1.1(c) lists only "The following Ridgeline dry kibble products" (RL-D and RL-C SKUs). APA §2.3 says Buyer assumes "all Liabilities arising out of or relating to the Purchased Assets or the operation of the Business, whether arising before, on or after the Closing, other than the Excluded Liabilities." Schedule 3.14 item 1 discloses a pending FDA inquiry into vitamin D levels in Copperpot canned food, with 4,200 cases on quality hold.
results.reason: The seller-retains product liability carve-out in §2.4(d) is tied to the defined term 'Products.' That term is limited to the Ridgeline dry kibble SKUs, even though the Business sold to Gleigen also includes the Copperpot retort-canned line and private-label manufacturing. §2.3 is a broad catch-all that makes Gleigen assume every pre-Closing Business liability not expressly excluded. As a result, pre-Closing Copperpot (and private-label) product liability and recall exposure becomes an Assumed Liability of Gleigen. That includes exposure from the live FDA vitamin D inquiry. Nothing in the folder cures this: (1) §8.2(c) indemnity covers only Excluded Liabilities. (2) The Copperpot FDA inquiry is disclosed on Schedule 3.14, so it qualifies §3.14 and cannot support a rep-breach claim. (3) Under §8.3(b), Gleigen must indemnify Seller for Assumed Liabilities. The LOI shows the intended deal was for Seller to keep all pre-closing product liability and recall exposure, so this is a drafting gap that harms the Buyer, not a deliberate allocation. The folder does not show that Closing has occurred, and the outside date (Dec 31, 2026) has not passed. Gleigen can still fix the definition (e.g., define Products as all products of the Business, including Copperpot and private-label) or seek a specific indemnity before Closing.

results.evidence: APA Section 7.2(c): "Seller has obtained, and delivered to Buyer copies of, each of the following (the "Required Consents"): (i) the written consent of the landlord under the Topeka Facility Lease to the assignment of the Topeka Facility Lease to Buyer; and (ii) the approval of the Kansas Department of Agriculture of the transfer to Buyer of Seller's commercial feed license for the Business, or the issuance to Buyer of a replacement license". Schedule 3.5, Part A, item 1: "Under Section 14.2, Fernhollow's prior written consent is required for any assignment of the agreement by Seller, including by operation of law or by change of control of Seller. If consent is not given, Fernhollow may terminate the agreement on 30 days' written notice to Seller. Consent has not been obtained as of the date of this Disclosure Schedule."
results.reason: The problem is present and hurts Gleigen as Buyer. Read together, the documents show the following gap. Schedule 3.5 discloses that Fernhollow's consent is required for the Fernhollow Private Label Manufacturing Agreement, which is an Assigned Contract. It also says that consent has not been obtained. The LOI shows this contract produces about 41% of the Business's revenue. Nothing in the APA protects Gleigen against that gap. (1) Section 7.2(c) limits the Required Consents to the landlord consent and the Kansas Department of Agriculture approval. (2) Section 5.3 obliges Seller to seek only the Required Consents, so Seller has no covenant to obtain Fernhollow's consent. (3) Section 2.8 provides that an unconsented contract stays with Seller "with no reduction in the Purchase Price." (4) The bring-down condition in Section 7.2(a) gives no protection, because Section 10.8 makes the schedule disclosure qualify the Section 3.5 representation. The missing consent is therefore not a breach, and Gleigen would have no indemnity claim. (5) The MAE condition is unlikely to be triggered, because Fernhollow's termination right would only be exercised after closing. As a result, Gleigen could be bound to close and pay the full $86.5 million without the largest customer contract. The ancillary agreements are still undated and the outside date is December 31, 2026, so the deal has not closed. The issue remains actionable: Gleigen can seek to add Fernhollow's consent as a closing condition or covenant, or seek a price adjustment.

Counting 270 days back from March 31, 2027 gives July 4, 2026, which is about six weeks before the August 14, 2026 signing date shown in the schedule. Schedule 3.9 describes the option and the lease status (in force, no default, rent current) but never says the option was exercised. On the schedule's own terms, the window to extend had already closed when the deal was signed. So an associate could see that Buyer is buying a business whose only plant lease ends in about seven months with no renewal right, which plainly hurts the client. What the schedule does not show: (1) the APA Section 5.9 covenant requiring Seller to 'timely exercise' the option, which would show the covenant cannot be performed; (2) whether Section 7.2(c) landlord consent might bring an extension; and (3) the board consent showing Gleigen relied on occupancy through 2032. Those facts only sharpen the issue. The expired option, and the harm it does to Buyer, can be seen from this document alone.
